periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Opening the Case: Pre-reading and Story Entry

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.101): pre-reading crossword and matching meanings of 'case'.

time_bands.activity: Invite students to share what they know about mystery stories and detectives. Briefly discuss what makes a good mystery: clues, codes, and a clever solver.
Students work the anagram crossword from “Let us read” (p.101) in pairs, then share answers aloud. Draw attention to how rearranging letters reveals hidden words — a skill central to the story.
Whole-class matching activity: students match the four meanings of ‘case’ (situation, matter, container, writing format) to the given sentences, discussing why English words carry multiple meanings.
Teacher reads the opening pages of the story aloud (p.101–104) while students follow in their books, pausing briefly after each paragraph to check understanding of setting and characters.

periods.teacher_notes: The anagram crossword primes students for the code-breaking at the story’s heart; linger on any anagram students find difficult before moving to the text. A common pitfall is treating the multiple meanings of ‘case’ as a vocabulary drill rather than a gateway to the story’s title — connect each meaning explicitly to the narrative. Students who find the crossword too easy may be invited to create their own anagram clue for a word of their choice.
materials: Class copies of the textbook, pp.101–104
Blackboard or whiteboard

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Inside the Investigation: Comprehension and Character

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.104): complete four sentence starters with reasons about Leroy, Chief Brown, and Nolan.
Let us discuss (p.108): match textual evidence to Leroy’s character traits from the given box.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.104): write whether Chief Brown needs Leroy’s help and why.

time_bands.activity: Briefly recap the story’s opening: Leroy’s encyclopaedic knowledge, the Diamond Mart heist five years earlier, and Tim Nolan’s death. Invite one student to describe what Chief Brown found at the nursery.

Students complete the four sentence starters from “Let us discuss” (p.104) individually, then compare answers with a partner. Facilitate a brief class discussion on each: why Leroy earned his nickname, why Chief Brown stared at his soup, and what Nolan’s will revealed.

Students work the character-traits matching table from “Let us discuss” (p.108): matching textual evidence to cleverness, humbleness, or keen-listener. Discuss each trait and ask students to supply one additional example from the story.

Set homework: students write a short personal response to the question of whether Chief Brown would need Leroy’s help (p.104), giving at least one reason. Clarify what a well-supported opinion looks like.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the opening pages of the story together, students now move from surface recall to reasoning about character and motive. Watch for students who conflate fact and opinion when completing the sentence starters. The character-traits table can reveal whether students are reading the story as plot alone or also attending to characterisation.
materials: Class copies of the textbook, pp.104–108
Blackboard or whiteboard

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Cracking the Code: Extract Analysis and Inference

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.107): identify eight statements as facts or opinions about the story.
Let us think and reflect (p.109): read Extract 1 and answer questions on Chief Brown’s dilemma and Leroy’s modesty.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the fact-versus-opinion distinction with two examples from everyday life. Students then work through all eight statements from “Let us think and reflect” (p.107) in pairs, labelling each fact or opinion and sharing their reasoning aloud.

Read Extract 1 (p.109) aloud as a class — the passage about Chief Brown’s dilemma and Leroy’s quiet modesty. Students then answer the four questions: completing the sentence about Chief Brown’s unique dilemma, the inference MCQ about Leroy’s silence, the MCQ on why parents use his real name, and the meaning of ‘stuck with’.
Class discussion: what does it mean to blend in? Students share whether they would want to be known for a special talent or prefer to keep it private, connecting to Leroy’s choice.
Brief consolidation: students write one sentence explaining what the phrase ‘stuck with a nickname’ means in their own words and share with a partner.

periods.teacher_notes: The fact-vs-opinion exercise from “Let us think and reflect” requires students to evaluate statements about a real police procedure and Leroy’s character — make sure students justify their labels with textual evidence rather than personal feeling. Extract 1 rewards slow, close reading: Leroy’s modesty is shown through action and silence rather than stated directly, so guide students to notice what the text does not say. Students who finish early may consider what the story would look like if Leroy were boastful.
materials: Class copies of the textbook, pp.107–109
Blackboard or whiteboard

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Decoding the Message: Extract 2 and Extended Response

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.109–110): read Extract 2 on the four-word code and answer four questions.
Let us think and reflect (p.110): answer selected extended questions on Nolan–Davenport relationship, Mrs Brown, and Chief Brown.

time_bands.activity: Read Extract 2 aloud — the scene where Chief Brown and Mrs Brown try and fail to decode ‘Nom Utes Sweden Hurts’ (p.109). Students answer the four questions: Chief Brown’s reaction MCQ, the true/false on Mrs Brown’s approach, the SCR on what her failure suggests, and the MCQ on Encyclopedia’s reminder.

Students work in pairs on the extended questions from “Let us think and reflect” (p.110): what evidence shows Nolan and Davenport were close; what Mrs Brown’s interest in the case reveals about her; why Chief Brown was proud of his son. Pairs share their answers with the class and the teacher moderates discussion.

Whole-class walkthrough of Leroy’s code solution: write ‘Nom Utes Sweden Hurts’ on the board and invite students to reconstruct the logic step by step — removing ‘day’ from each word. Discuss the fifth word ‘Fir’ and why it pointed to the young fir tree on the south side of the nursery.
Students write one sentence in their notebooks on why pattern recognition — noticing what is missing, not what is present — was the key to solving this case.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through character and fact-opinion in earlier units, students now apply inferential reading to the coded message itself. A common difficulty is distinguishing Mrs Brown’s literal analysis of the words from Leroy’s structural analysis of the code pattern; use the board to make the two approaches visible side by side. Students who are drawn to the cryptographic logic may be pointed toward the ‘Let us explore’ section on optical illusions and word puzzles as a self-study extension.
materials: Class copies of the textbook, pp.109–110
Blackboard or whiteboard

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Listening Carefully and Speaking with Purpose

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.117): listen to the observation-skills podcast and mark four statements true or false.
Let us speak (p.117): group discussion on ‘The Interesting Aspects of a Mystery Story’ with turn-taking phrases.

homework.task_brief: Let us listen (p.117): re-listen mentally and fill five blanks with exact words from the podcast transcript.

time_bands.activity: Set the listening context: tell students they will hear a short podcast on improving observation skills — the same kind of attentiveness that made Leroy a great detective. Ask them to read the four true/false statements (p.117) silently before listening begins.

Read the podcast transcript aloud at a natural pace (p.151). Students mark each of the four statements true or false individually, then compare with a neighbour before the teacher provides answers and brief justification for each verdict.
Bridge to speaking: students note down two observation tips from the podcast that they think Leroy uses in the story. One or two students share their links aloud.

Form groups of five or six for the guided group discussion on ‘The Interesting Aspects of a Mystery Story’ (p.117). Each group appoints a moderator who opens the discussion, manages turn-taking using the given phrases (agree, disagree, interrupt politely), and sums up. Teacher circulates, noting who leads and who holds back, and encourages quieter voices.

periods.teacher_notes: The podcast’s five techniques — slowing down, engaging all senses, asking questions, taking notes, and practising mindfulness — map directly onto Leroy’s quiet, systematic method; naming those links rewards careful listeners. In the group discussion, watch for students who dominate: remind the moderator role to call explicitly on those who have not yet spoken, as the NCF pedagogy notes that some students hesitate for socio-cultural reasons and need structured invitation. The fill-in-the-blanks homework task requires students to recall exact words from the podcast, so advise them to jot key phrases during the listening phase.
materials: Class copies of the textbook, pp.117 and p.151 (transcript)
Blackboard or whiteboard

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Pronunciation, Then a Report in Writing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.117): practise pronunciation of story words and a further set using the guide.
Let us write (p.117): study the sample report format and draft a report on an inter-school art exhibition.

time_bands.activity: Pronunciation practice: teacher models each word from “Let us speak” (p.117) — jewellery, clerk, dessert — using the guide in brackets, then the additional set (January, sour, pizza, Wednesday, bowl, buffet, pronunciation). Students repeat chorally and then in pairs, with the teacher circulating to correct individual errors.

Examine the sample football tournament report on the board or in the textbook: identify the title with byline, the what/who/when/where opening paragraph, the sequenced body paragraphs, and the prize-giving closing. Students label each section in their books.

Students draft their own report on an inter-school art exhibition as a member of the Art and Craft Club (“Let us write”, p.117). They follow the four-paragraph structure identified above: title and byline, event details, description with sequence markers, and closing remarks. Teacher circulates and gives formative feedback on structure and register.

Students swap reports with a partner and check that all four structural elements are present. One or two volunteers read their opening paragraph aloud. Teacher offers brief feedback on formal register.

periods.teacher_notes: Pronunciation of ‘Wednesday’ and ‘jewellery’ regularly trips up students — spend a moment on each and invite students to suggest words they find difficult to pronounce before moving on. The sample report format is the model: students should not invent their own structure but work within the four-section scaffold provided. A common lapse in functional writing is shifting into informal register mid-report; point out specific phrases in the sample that signal formality.
materials: Class copies of the textbook, pp.117 (speaking) and p.117 (writing sample)
Blackboard or whiteboard
Notebooks for drafting

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Phrasal Verbs, Homophones, and Word Play

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.111): match six phrasal verbs to meanings, then fill blanks in six sentences.
Let us learn (p.111–112): fill correct homophone pairs into five sentences.
Let us learn (p.113): solve spoonerisms and find the original phrases.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.112): solve the visual word puzzles and infer what each says.

time_bands.activity: Students match the six phrasal verbs from the story (put on, cooled down, turned up, make of, figure out, got away with) to their meanings from “Let us learn” (p.111), using context prediction before confirming with a dictionary. They then complete the six fill-in-the-blank sentences using the correct phrasal verb.

Introduce homophones using the story’s link: Leroy spotted what was hidden inside familiar-looking words. Students complete the five homophone-pair sentences (p.111–112) individually, then check with a partner by reading each sentence aloud to hear which word sounds right in context.

Introduce spoonerism as a playful sound swap (p.113). Read a couple of examples aloud so students hear the first-sound exchange. In pairs, students work out the original phrases for all eight spoonerisms, writing their answers and comparing across pairs.
Set homework: students examine the visual word puzzles (p.112) at home and write the phrase or idea each puzzle represents, bringing answers for a quick class share.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit covers the vocabulary and grammar spine in an isolated period, as the constitution requires. The homophones task benefits from being read aloud — students who only read silently often choose the wrong word; insist on reading completed sentences aloud with a partner. Spoonerisms are unfamiliar to most students: model the sound-swap rule on the board with one example before releasing pairs to the remaining seven. Students who finish spoonerisms early may try composing a spoonerism of their own.
materials: Class copies of the textbook, pp.111–113
Dictionaries (one per pair or small group)
Blackboard or whiteboard

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Conjunctions, Reported Speech, and Grammar in Action

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.113): fill blanks in a detective-story paragraph with relative and subordinating conjunctions.
Let us learn (p.115): transform five direct-speech questions to indirect speech using the given sentence starters.
Let us learn (p.116): rewrite six direct-speech sentences in reported speech.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.114): combine three sentence pairs using the conjunction given in brackets.

time_bands.activity: Students read the detective-story paragraph from “Let us learn” (p.113) and fill in the eight blanks using the box of relative and subordinating conjunctions (where, why, who, though, which, when, because, whose, if, how). Teacher draws attention to examples from the story text that use the same conjunctions.

Teach the rules for transforming direct to indirect speech for questions: tense shift, pronoun change, time-place change, and the if/whether pattern for yes/no questions. Students then complete the five sentences (p.115) using the given starters (Mrs. Brown asked…, Mrs. Brown questioned Leroy…, etc.).

Students rewrite the six direct-speech sentences in reported speech (p.116) independently. Teacher circulates, focusing feedback on verb tense accuracy and the omission of question marks in indirect questions. Two or three answers are shared and corrected on the board.
Set homework: combine the three sentence pairs using the conjunction in brackets (p.114). Remind students that the conjunction must connect, not simply join, the two ideas.

periods.teacher_notes: The conjunction cloze is manageable only if students understand the semantic distinction between relative (who, which, whose, where, when) and subordinating (though, because, if, how, why) conjunctions — spend a moment on this before the exercise. A persistent error in reported speech is forgetting to shift the tense and dropping question-mark punctuation; the six rewriting sentences offer multiple instances to practise both simultaneously. Students who conflate direct and indirect question forms may benefit from reading their reported sentences aloud to notice where they sound unnatural.
materials: Class copies of the textbook, pp.113–116
Blackboard or whiteboard

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Exploring Further: Optical Illusions, Word Games, and the Library

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.117): examine optical illusions and discuss how perception can deceive the eye.
Let us explore (p.117): play the ‘Name the Mystery Object’ language game in teams with hint-based scoring.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p.117): visit the library, locate an encyclopedia, and note how it differs from a dictionary.

time_bands.activity: Display or point to the optical illusion images from “Let us explore” (p.117). Students look carefully and record what they see first, then what they see on second look. Brief class discussion: how does this connect to the way Leroy noticed what others missed in the coded message?

Divide the class into teams of four or five for the ‘Name the Mystery Object’ game (p.117). Each team chooses an object and prepares three hints before their turn; teams earn 20, 10, or 5 points depending on how many hints the guessing team needs. Teacher acts as timekeeper and moderator, ensuring every team presents.

Brief reflection: students name one skill from the game — careful word choice, listening for detail, narrowing down possibilities — that also appears in Encyclopedia Brown’s method of solving the case.

Set library homework: students will visit the library, locate an encyclopedia, and bring back a short note on how it differs from a dictionary. Remind them that the chapter’s hero earned his nickname precisely because of this kind of reference knowledge.

periods.teacher_notes: The optical illusion activity is brief but purposeful: it primes students to question what they see at first glance, which is the perceptual habit the story celebrates. The word game rewards careful hint construction — teams who prepare vague hints quickly learn that precision matters more than length. The library task is assigned as homework because it requires access outside the classroom; students who do not have library access may use a classroom dictionary and an available reference book to compare structure instead.
materials: Class copies of the textbook, p.117
Blackboard or whiteboard for scorekeeping
Prepared object cards (optional) or students choose their own objects

items.source_section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
items.source_lo: Student reads a prose narrative closely to identify stated facts, infer character motivation, and analyse how coded language drives plot, using the mystery story as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Leroy’s code-breaking, Chief Brown’s dilemma, Nolan–Davenport heist, four-word day-name cipher hiding stolen jewellery.
items.item_stem:
Read the following statements about the Diamond Mart robbery and Tim Nolan. Write True or False for each statement and give a one-sentence reason drawn from the story.
1. The Diamond Mart robbery took place on Sixth Avenue, and one of the two masked robbers had his mask slip during the hold-up.
2. Police found the stolen jewellery hidden inside Nolan’s palm-tree nursery during the morning search after his death.
3. Nolan and Davenport were suspected as partners in the robbery because they had met while both were serving time in prison.
4. Davenport was arrested shortly after the jewellery heist and was available for questioning by Chief Brown.

options.text: Davenport was arrested shortly after the jewellery heist and was available for questioning by Chief Brown.
Nolan and Davenport were suspected as partners in the robbery because they had met while both were serving time in prison.
Police found the stolen jewellery hidden inside Nolan’s palm-tree nursery during the morning search after his death.
The Diamond Mart robbery took place on Sixth Avenue, and one of the two masked robbers had his mask slip during the hold-up.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. True — the story states two masked men held up the Diamond Mart on Sixth Avenue and one mask slipped, though the clerk was not certain enough to testify. 2. False — officers searched the nursery in the morning and found nothing; the jewellery was later found inside a jug of earth holding the young fir tree, after Leroy decoded the message. 3. True — the story records that Nolan and Davenport had met while both were in prison in South Carolina. 4. False — Davenport disappeared right after the robbery and was never found or arrested.

items.source_section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
items.source_lo: Student reads a prose narrative closely to identify stated facts, infer character motivation, and analyse how coded language drives plot, using the mystery story as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Leroy’s code-breaking, Chief Brown’s dilemma, Nolan–Davenport heist, four-word day-name cipher hiding stolen jewellery.
items.item_stem: The four words on Nolan’s desk calendar — ‘Nom Utes Sweden Hurts’ — were a code that only Leroy could decipher, while both Chief Brown and Mrs Brown failed. Analyse why Mrs Brown’s approach to the code was inadequate, and explain in a short paragraph how Leroy’s method of reading the words was fundamentally different. Use evidence from the story to support your answer.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Mrs Brown interpreted each word by its literal dictionary meaning (nominative, an American Indian tribe, a European country, and the verb hurts) and could not find a connection. Leroy looked at the words as a structural pattern: he noticed that removing the letters ‘d’, ‘a’, and ‘y’ from each word yielded a day of the week (Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday), and inferred that the unwritten fifth word ‘Fir’ stood for Friday — the location of the hiding place. His insight was that the code exploited what was removed, not what was present.

items.source_section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
items.source_lo: Student listens to an informational podcast to distinguish accurate from inaccurate claims and to retrieve precise words and phrases, using focused listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Podcast on five observation-skill techniques: slowing down, engaging senses, asking questions, taking notes, mindfulness.
items.item_stem: The podcast ‘Improving Your Observation Skills’ describes five techniques for becoming a better observer. Which of the following accurately states what the podcast says about the benefit of taking notes or making sketches?

options.label: A
options.text: It helps you share your observations with other people more clearly.

options.label: B
options.text: It reinforce details in your memory and strengthens your understanding of features.

options.label: C
options.text: It replaces the need to practise mindfulness in daily life.

options.label: D
options.text: It trains you to slow down and engage all five senses at once.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the social purpose of communication with the memory-reinforcement purpose the podcast states for note-taking.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Merges two separate techniques — slowing down and engaging senses — into the note-taking tip, suggesting the student did not track each tip distinctly.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Inverts the podcast’s message; mindfulness is listed as an additional, separate technique, not one that note-taking replaces.

items.item_stem:
The podcast states that observation involves more than just seeing. Based on what the podcast says, fill in the blanks with the exact words or phrases from the transcript.
1. The host says that observation skills can help us become more aware, make better decisions, and even _______________.
2. According to the host, asking questions forces your brain to _______________ about what you are observing.
3. The host says that mindfulness helps you stay _______________ in the moment and fully engage with your surroundings.

items.item_stem: Your teacher will read the following words aloud one at a time: jewellery, clerk, Wednesday, buffet, dessert. After hearing each word, say it back clearly and then use it in a spoken sentence about the story or about mystery writing in general.

expected_elements: Accurate pronunciation of each word matching the guide (e.g., ‘jool-ree’, ‘claak’).
Sentence uses the word in a meaningful context related to the story or mystery genre.
Student speaks with audible clarity and appropriate pace.
No significant mispronunciation of silent letters (e.g., silent ‘d’ in Wednesday).

items.item_stem: In a group of five, hold a discussion on the topic ‘What makes a mystery story satisfying to read?’ One student acts as moderator and opens the discussion. Each speaker must use at least one polite expression to agree or disagree with a previous speaker, and must refer to at least one specific detail from ‘The Case of the Fifth Word’ to support their view. The moderator closes by summarising the group’s main points.

expected_elements: Moderator opens and closes discussion with a clear summary.
Each speaker uses at least one polite agreement or disagreement expression.
At least one story-specific detail cited (e.g., the coded message, Leroy’s one question).
All group members are given a turn; no single speaker dominates.

items.item_stem: As the secretary of your school’s Science Club, write a report on an ‘Inter-school Science Quiz’ held at your school. Use the four-part structure: a title with your name as reporter, an opening paragraph with what/who/when/where details, a body of one or two paragraphs with sequence markers describing how the event unfolded, and a closing paragraph on the prize-giving and concluding remarks.

expected_elements: Title present with reporter’s name as byline.
Opening paragraph covers what, who, when, and where of the event.
Body uses sequence markers (first, then, next, finally) to describe events.
Closing paragraph mentions prize-giving and a concluding remark in formal register.

items.source_lo: Student plans and drafts a formal report in a prescribed four-part structure, using functional writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Report on an inter-school art exhibition: title with byline, event details paragraph, descriptive body with sequence markers, prize-giving closing.
items.item_stem: You have just read how Leroy Brown, the modest boy genius, solved a case his father’s entire police department could not crack. Write a short opinion piece (150–180 words) for your school magazine arguing whether you think a person’s quiet, unassuming manner — like Leroy’s — is a strength or a weakness in today’s world. Support your opinion with at least one example from the story and one from your own experience or observation.

expected_elements: Clear opinion stated in the opening sentence or paragraph.
At least one specific reference to Leroy’s behaviour in the story (e.g., not boasting, blending in).
A personal example or observation that develops the argument.
Appropriate magazine-writing register: semi-formal, engaging, not conversational.

items.visual_stimulus:
Phrasal Verb | Meaning
figure out | (i) appeared or been discovered
cooled down | (ii) escaped without being punished
turned up | (iii) work out the answer to something
make of | (iv) became calm or returned to normal
got away with | (v) have an understanding or opinion of something

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: figure out – (iii); cooled down – (iv); turned up – (i); make of – (v); got away with – (ii).

answer_key.right: (iii) work out the answer to something
(iv) became calm or returned to normal
(v) have an understanding or opinion of something

items.source_lo: Student applies knowledge of phrasal verbs, homophones, subordinating conjunctions, and direct-to-indirect speech transformation, using the story’s language as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Phrasal verbs from the story text; homophone pairs; subordinating and relative conjunctions; reported speech transformation of interrogative sentences.
items.item_stem: In the story, Chief Brown asks his wife a question in direct speech. Imagine he said: ‘Can you figure out what the four words mean?’ Transform this question into indirect (reported) speech, making all necessary changes to tense, pronoun, and word order. Then write one original sentence using a subordinating conjunction (choose from: because, though, when, if) to explain why Leroy was able to solve the case when his parents could not.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Chief Brown asked his wife if she could figure out what the four words meant. (Accept minor variation in reporting verb.) Example sentence using a subordinating conjunction: Leroy succeeded because he looked for a structural pattern in the words rather than their literal meanings. (Accept other valid conjunctions and logically accurate sentences.)

items.item_stem: Optical illusions show us that what we see at first glance is not always accurate. Write a short paragraph (4–5 sentences) explaining how this idea connects to Leroy’s method of solving the code in ‘The Case of the Fifth Word’. In your paragraph, name one specific moment in the story where looking beneath the surface — rather than accepting the obvious — was the key to finding the truth.

expected_elements: Connects optical illusions to the idea that first impressions can mislead.
Names a specific story moment (e.g., the four words looking like ordinary nouns).
Explains how Leroy’s structural approach revealed what was hidden beneath the surface.
Paragraph is logically organised and 4–5 sentences in length.

items.item_stem: Design a project titled ‘Patterns Hidden in Plain Sight’. Your project must include three parts: (1) Create your own four-word code (using the same method Leroy decoded — hiding a common word inside another word) and write a brief explanation of how your code works. (2) Choose any five words and find two synonyms for each using a thesaurus, presenting your findings in a labelled table. (3) Write a short note (5–6 sentences) on how reference tools like encyclopedias and thesauruses help a reader go beyond surface understanding of a text, using Leroy’s nickname and his encyclopaedic knowledge as your starting point.

expected_elements: Original four-word code constructed using a word-hiding or letter-removal pattern.
Thesaurus table correctly lists five words each with two valid synonyms.
Note connects reference tools to deeper reading using Leroy’s knowledge as an example.
All three parts are clearly labelled and presented in an organised format.
